A Scientific Claim Stability Framework for Evaluating MRI Morphometry Pipelines
summary: MRI morphometry pipelines are often evaluated by measurement agreement or downstream accuracy, yet their scientific value depends on the conclusions they support. Two pipelines can produce similar feature-level results yet support different conclusions about aging, cognitive decline, or neurodegeneration. We introduce Scientific Claim Stability (SCS), a claim-centric evaluation framework that converts region-of-interest (ROI) morphometry tables into auditable claim cards and evaluates their support under changes in dataset, processing pipeline, atlas, feature family, and target. Across 10,370 MRI scans from three datasets and five cohorts, SCS generates 2,783 claim cards and evaluates 89 claim-family pairs. The evaluation distinguishes stable, transferable, and fragile claims. FreeSurfer 8-FastSurfer comparisons show high evidence concordance and low anatomical-support overlap under the primary covariate specification. Acquisition-adjusted analyses show that the magnitude of support disagreement depends on the model specification. Structured review by specialists in geriatrics, neuroscience, and radiology, alongside auxiliary ChatGPT and Gemini reviewers, assesses claim plausibility, clarity, faithfulness, usefulness, and caution. SCS provides a reproducible way to audit the evidential stability of morphometry claims without assuming a universal gold standard.

MRI-free OPM-MEG recovers medial temporal lobe theta during scene imagination
summary: Optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) offers a wearable, movement-tolerant alternative to conventional cryogenic MEG, placing sensors closer to the scalp and, in principle, improving sensitivity to deep sources. This is advantageous for examining subcortical structures that are affected by ageing, disorders and disease, such as the hippocampus. However, it remains unclear whether well-established activity (such as the attenuation of theta oscillations during the imagination of novel scenes) can be recovered from the medial temporal lobe (MTL) with OPM-MEG, and whether an individual structural MRI is required. Here, fifteen adults completed a scene imagination task. Initially we applied a 12-parameter template warping coregistration pipeline to the full sample. Following source reconstruction, we recovered the expected attenuation of theta (4-8 Hz) power during scene imagination compared to a counting baseline, with a significant cluster of activity peaking in the left parahippocampal gyrus. The clusters centre of mass was localised to the left hippocampus (t = -3.55, p = 0.048, whole-brain FWE-corrected) and was mostly confined to the left medial temporal lobe. We further supported our findings by using an individual T1-weighted MRI reconstruction pipeline in six participants who had these scans available. The two approaches produced similar whole-brain topographies and localised the peak MTL theta effect to left hippocampus, with temporal-lobe conjunction centroids 3-mm apart. These findings provide evidence that the theta attenuation of the scene construction network can be recovered at the group level with OPM-MEG, without an individual MRI.

title: Mitochondrial genome editing reveals the impact of complex I heteroplasmic variants on human neurogenesis
summary: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants, whether maternally inherited or acquired somatically during aging, can be particularly detrimental to cells that rely on mitochondrial metabolism such as neurons. The functional consequences of mtDNA variants are thought to depend on their heteroplasmy, defined as the proportion of mtDNA molecules carrying that variant. However, investigating the specific effects of heteroplasmic mtDNA variants on human neuronal function has been challenging. Studies using patient-derived cells cannot conclusively attribute observed phenotypes to a single mtDNA variant, while conventional genome editing approaches are not applicable to mtDNA. Here, we use DddA-derived cytosine base editor (DdCBE) to introduce pathogenic heteroplasmic mtDNA variants into Neurogenin 2 (NGN2)-inducible human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We focus on two variants in the genes MT-ND1 and MT-ND5 belonging to complex I (CI), the largest component of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and a frequent contributor to human disease, including the incurable neurodevelopmental disorder Leigh syndrome. mtDNA-edited iPSC lines exhibit low off-target editing and maintain similar heteroplasmy following subclonal isolation and differentiation into NGN2-induced neurons (iNs). Although the CI variants do not substantially affect mitochondrial energy metabolism in undifferentiated iPSCs, they reduce mitochondrial membrane potential in iNs where they drive a transcriptional reprogramming indicative of impaired neuronal commitment. These findings suggest that heteroplasmic CI variants are sufficient to disrupt neural fate specification even at relatively low heteroplasmy. More broadly, mtDNA editing in human iPSCs provides a powerful platform to investigate how mitochondrial fitness and heteroplasmy influence development and disease.

title: Reduced cerebral blood flow and metabolic rate trigger an adaptive mitochondrial remodeling program in a Down syndrome mouse model
summary: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a central feature of Down syndrome (DS), yet how trisomy 21 affects brain bioenergetics across scales--from gene transcription to cellular function to whole-brain metabolism--remains poorly understood. Here, we use the Dp16(1)Yey/+ (abbreviated Dp16) DS mouse model, which carries ~115 triplicated gene orthologs of human chromosome 21, to address this major knowledge gap and to provide direct in vivo evidence of brain-wide metabolic deficit in DS. Using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) approaches, we show that Dp16 mice have reduced cerebral blood flow and metabolic rate of oxygen, with effects more pronounced in males than in females. Despite the suppression of cerebral metabolic rate, mitochondrial respiratory capacity and ATP synthase activity are largely preserved across brain regions, with sex differences noted. Transcriptomic analyses reveal marked upregulation of mitochondrial OXPHOS genes and the convergence of biological pathways related to proteostasis and mitochondrial function across brain regions, with male cortex and female cerebellum showing the biggest change. Collectively, our data suggest that a brain-wide metabolic deficit in Dp16 mice triggers an adaptive mitochondrial remodeling program across the brain to support bioenergetic demands. This compensatory response, however, is insufficient to normalize the metabolic dysfunction in Dp16 mice. Our findings underscore the value of integrating functional assessments at the organismal and tissue levels with transcriptomic changes to gain a systems view of physiologic perturbations and adaptations in the DS brain which may influence phenotypic outcomes.

title: Spatial and developmental reprogramming enables root growth under high salinity
summary: How do plant roots sustain growth under salinity levels that would normally arrest development? The extremophyte Schrenkiella parvula maintains root growth under high salinity through a previously unrecognized spatial reorganization of primary root development. The root elongation zone transitions into two distinct developmental states, the bulged and gap zones, during a transient growth pause that precedes renewed tip growth and localized lateral root emergence. In Arabidopsis, a related salt-sensitive species, the cells in the elongation zone simply burst. Jasmonic acid was found to be necessary to initiate this transition in S. parvula, while spatially coordinated jasmonic acid and auxin accumulation accompanies zone establishment and maintenance. We constructed zone-resolved transcriptomic networks to distinguish developmental from salt-responsive processes and identified their interactions under salinity stress. Salt-induced zone-specific networks revealed distinct regulatory programs coordinating hormone signaling, cell wall remodeling, and water, ion, and reactive oxygen species homeostasis. Cell layer-specific Raman spectroscopy, UHPLC-MS/MS metabolite profiling, and cellular imaging provide independent support for the transcriptomic networks, linking spatially organized cellular responses with salt stress mitigation, suppression of cell death, and continued growth. We also identified orthologous genes potentially recruited into novel regulatory roles that support growth under stress. Together, these findings establish spatial developmental reprogramming as a strategy for sustaining root growth under salinity and identify candidate mechanisms for improving crop salt tolerance.

title: Disrupting SORL1-retromer endosomal recycling in mice drives the age-dependent neurodegenerative signature of Alzheimer's disease
summary: MRI studies have mapped the atrophic signature that distinguishes Alzheimer's disease (AD), isolating regions differentially vulnerable to its age-dependent neurodegenerative process. An endosomal recycling pathway regulated by the interaction of SORL1 with retromer is pathogenically disrupted in AD. Here we test the hypothesis, that the pathway might drive the neurodegenerative process, via multiple yearlong studies in over 140 wildtype and SORL1 deficient mice, modeling SORL1's causative mutations. MRI studies revealed that SORL1 deficiency induced an age-dependent AD-pattern of atrophy, centered on the trans-entorhinal cortex, and that atrophy was prevented by SORL1 restoration, secondary to overexpressing the retromer protein VPS26b. Postmortem studies validated that the atrophy reflects neuronal loss. Proteomic profiling revealed that the atrophy is associated with reductions in cell death suppressors, one of which was then found deficient in the trans-entorhinal cortex of AD patients. Besides supporting the hypothesis, when taken together with other findings the results suggest that SORL1-retromer disruptions represent a therapeutically-amenable common 'neurodegeneration pathway' in AD.

title: Activity drives local CaMKII synthesis and subcellular localization via autophosphorylation-dependent pathways
summary: Strong repeated stimulation of a neuron triggers an increase in local protein synthesis along with a change in localization of proteins, allowing the neuron to rapidly adjust its proteome in response to activity. One of these proteins, calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), is involved in mediating structural and functional changes after activity. While postsynaptic CaMKII translation has been studied, very little is known about presynaptic synthesis, including its mechanisms and the functional consequences. We utilized the Drosophila larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ) as a model to study the molecular requirements for activity-dependent synthesis along with the localization of CaMKII protein. Presynaptic-specific tagging of endogenous CaMKII demonstrates that spaced stimulation rapidly increases presynaptic CaMKII through local translation of pre-existing mRNA, independently of somatic factors. This activity-dependent synthesis requires the distal 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of the CaMKII mRNA, which is also necessary for steady-state synaptic accumulation. Additionally, we show that activity-dependent synthesis requires CaMKII T287 autophosphorylation-induced activation of the PI3K/Akt/mTor pathway. While activity-dependent redistribution of CaMKII has been previously identified, very little is known about how local synthesis and translocation may interact to define different pools of protein that may have distinct functions. We demonstrate that CaMKII with a T287D phosphomimetic mutant localizes to the synaptic membrane and pulse-chase experiments show that the localization of newly-synthesized CaMKII differs from pre-existing CaMKII, indicating neuronal activity generates spatially distinct, and likely functionally distinct, CaMKII populations which may underlie long-lasting plasticity.
